title: When a Father Offered His Daughters to Be Abused — Genesis 19:6–8
paragraphs: When a Father Offered His Daughters to Be Abused — Genesis 19:6–8
He opened the door to protect strangers.

Genesis 19:6–8 does not celebrate Lot. It exposes how deep a city’s darkness had gone—and how twisted a compromised man can become even while trying to do one “right” thing. Lot was willing to guard his guests, yes. But he was also so shaped by Sodom’s corruption that he spoke an unthinkable evil over his own daughters. Scripture does not hide that filth. It shows it.

It does not only make people cruel. It makes people confused. Morally bent. Capable of calling one duty righteous while crushing another. Lot was not a hero in that moment. He was a warning. A man living too close to wickedness eventually starts thinking like it.

The horror of Genesis 19 is not there to entertain us. It is there to confront us. Because sin still bargains with innocence. Sin still sacrifices the vulnerable. Sin still tells men to protect reputation while abandoning responsibility. Sin still ruins homes before it ruins cities.
And that is why we need more than moral advice.

Jesus is everything Lot was not. He does not hand the innocent over to violence. He is the innocent One who gave Himself to save the guilty. He does not offer up the vulnerable to protect Himself. He lays down His own life to rescue the vulnerable, the shamed, the broken, and the ruined. At the cross, evil did its worst—but grace wrote the final word.
So do not read Genesis 19 and say, “How terrible.”
Read it and say, “Lord, how deep sin runs in us—and how desperately we need Christ.”

For the abused, Jesus sees.
For the compromised, Jesus calls to repent.
For the ashamed, Jesus still offers mercy.
For the home poisoned by sin, Jesus can rebuild what hell tried to devour.
But the Gospel shines brighter against ugly things.

Repent of compromise.
Come out of Sodom.
Run to Christ.
Because even where sin becomes monstrous, grace still speaks a stronger name.
